title: Configuration-based understanding of superradiant phase transitions in Dicke lattices
abstract: The emergence of multiple superradiant phases in Dicke lattice models has attracted considerable attention in the quantum optics community. However, a unified understanding of the origin of multistability and its relation to different superradiant phases is still lacking. Here, we develop a configuration-based understanding to classify the superradiant phases in Dicke lattices. We show that photon hopping naturally organizes the possible superradiant configurations according to the lattice symmetry, providing a unified interpretation of the nonequilibrium phase diagram and the emergence of multistability. For the dissipative four-site Dicke lattice, we obtain the complete phase diagram and identify the coexistence of up to four stable superradiant phases. The proposed classification is further extended to five- and six-site lattices. Moreover, we demonstrate that the same configuration-based understanding also applies to the closed Dicke lattice, where the ground state uniquely selects one of the allowed configurations. Finally, we show that different configurations may belong to either same or distinct nonequilibrium universality classes in the dissipative Dicke lattice, while they share the same equilibrium universality class in the closed Dicke lattice. Our results provide a unified picture for understanding equilibrium and nonequilibrium superradiant phase transitions in Dicke lattices.
summary: The paper introduces a configuration-based framework to unify the understanding of superradiant phase transitions in Dicke lattices. By classifying stable configurations based on lattice symmetry, it maps out complex, multi-stable phase diagrams for both open (dissipative) and closed quantum systems. This provides a comprehensive picture connecting local atomic/photonic arrangements to global thermodynamic behavior.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a unified, configuration-based understanding of how multistability arises and relates different superradiant phases in Dicke lattices.
main_result: The authors classify superradiant phases based on lattice symmetry configurations, demonstrating that the system can exhibit up to four stable phases for $N=4$ sites. They also contrast the behavior between dissipative (nonequilibrium) and closed (equilibrium) systems regarding universality classes.
method: The analysis employs a mean-field approach derived from the Lindblad master equation for the open system, supplemented by stability analysis via linearization around steady states. For equilibrium, ground state energy minimization is used.
model_or_system: The model is the Dicke lattice, consisting of coupled atom-resonator units on a 1D lattice ($N$ sites). The dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian and dissipation (Lindblad equation), incorporating photon hopping ($\xi$).
key_observables: Superradiant phases (NP vs. SRP), local order parameters ($R_j, I_j$), coexistence of stable steady states, and critical exponents ($\gamma_{open}, \gamma_{closed}$).
important_parameters: Photon hopping strength ($\xi$), dissipation rate ($\kappa$), coupling strengths ($g$), and lattice size ($N=4, 5, 6$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mean-field approximation for correlations ($\langle AB angle \simeq \langle A angle \langle B angle$) and sometimes uses the Discrete Truncated Wigner Approximation (DTWA).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate representative superradiant configurations for $N=5$ and $N=6$, and show scaling behavior of on-site fluctuations ($\Delta_j$) near critical couplings.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and then develops a configuration classification scheme. It analyzes the dissipative case to map out the phase diagram, followed by an extension to the closed lattice to compare equilibrium vs. nonequilibrium universality classes.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful structural tool (configuration-based understanding) to organize complex many-body dynamics in open quantum systems like cavity QED arrays, unifying disparate findings on multistability and phase transitions.
